list.listitem: Most patients with chronic aortic insufficiency (AI) remain asymptomatic for many years; symptoms of heart failure develop with the gradual decline in the function of the left ventricle. C
Diagnosis is usually made clinically on the basis of an early diastolic murmur and a wide pulse pressure. C
A transthoracic echocardiogram reliably establishes the diagnosis, severity, and mechanism of AI in most cases. C
Endocarditis prophylaxis is only indicated in selected patients with AI (post-transplant, prosthetic valve, history of endocarditis). B
Development of symptoms is associated with a poor prognosis and is an indication for aortic valve replacement. B
Vasodilator therapy can be considered in symptomatic patients who are not surgical candidates. C
Acute AI is a medical and surgical emergency and in the absence of prompt surgical intervention rapidly leads to shock and death. B

background.definition: Aortic insufficiency (AI) or aortic regurgitation is a valvular heart disease (VHD) characterized by abnormal reversal of blood flow from the aorta to the left ventricle through the aortic valve during diastole. AI results from inadequate closure of aortic valve leaflets or from dilatation of the aortic root.

list.listitem: In the Framingham Heart Study, AI had an overall prevalence of 4.7%. Prevalence of AI of moderate or greater severity was approximately 1 in 200 (0.5%).
Compared with the predominantly white Framingham cohort, AI is more prevalent in African Americans (15.6%) and Indian Americans (10%).
The prevalence of AI increases with age.
Aortic valve disorders (stenosis and insufficiency) are responsible for approximately 62% of the 20,000 deaths per year attributed to VHD in the Unites States.
Forty five percent of the 95,000 hospital admissions per year related to VHD are because of disorders of the aortic valve.
Rheumatic heart disease remains the leading cause of AI in low income countries.
In the United States and Western Europe, major causes of AI include aortic root disease (eg, annuloaortic ectasia and Marfan syndrome) and congenital bicuspid aortic valve.
Aortic insufficiency can develop after aortic valve replacement from prosthesis leaflet degeneration or from perivalvular leak.
Acute AI is less common and has multiple causes, including infective endocarditis, aortic dissection, and traumatic leaflet rupture.
A large percentage of patients have idiopathic AI. In 1 study, 91% of such individuals had systemic hypertension, suggesting a possible association.
Congenital bicuspid aortic valve is a risk factor for AI (odds ratio [OR] = 2.4; 95% CI, 1.6-3.6).
Regurgitant blood in AI results in both volume and pressure overload of the left ventricle.
In chronic AI, normal effective stroke volume is maintained early on by a compensatory increase in left ventricle end-diastolic volume.
With continued increase in left ventricle end-diastolic volume and pressure, and the resultant eccentric ventricular hypertrophy, left ventricle dysfunction eventually sets in.
The combination of decreases in diastolic pressure and effective stroke volume culminates in compromised coronary perfusion and subsequent myocardial ischemia.
Both left ventricular dysfunction and myocardial ischemia are responsible for development of symptomatic heart failure in patients with chronic AI.

In acute AI, the compensatory mechanisms are lacking. The left ventricle is unable to accommodate the sudden increase in volume and pressure. Therefore, profound hypotension and cardiogenic shock can develop rapidly in patients with acute AI of any cause.
Endocarditis prophylaxis is only indicated in selected patients with AI (post-transplant, prosthetic valve, history of endocarditis). B
Prevention involves appropriate treatment of group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis. A
The 2003 ACC/AHA guidelines recommend screening all patients with Marfan syndrome or other similar disorders that result in aortic root dilatation (eg, Ehler–Danlos syndrome, Loeys–Dietz syndrome).
Screening with echocardiography can be considered in first-degree relatives of patients in whom AI is due to Marfan syndrome.
Screening for aortic valve dysfunction and aortic root dilatation should be considered in patients with known bicuspid aortic valves and their first degree relatives.
Timely treatment of group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis with antibiotics reduces the incidence of rheumatic heart disease, the leading cause of AI in the developing world.

The only studies used IV or intramuscular antibiotics. Although oral regimens have been shown to result in clinical cure and bacterial eradication, there are no data on their effectiveness in preventing rheumatic fever.

The ACC/AHA 2008 guidelines recommend infective endocarditis prophylaxis for patients with AI in the following categories only: (1) valvular regurgitation in cardiac transplant patients; (2) prosthetic heart valves, or if prosthetic material was used for valve repair, or (3) a history of infective endocarditis.
In these patients, endocarditis prophylaxis is reasonable prior to procedures involving perforation of oral mucosa or manipulation of gingival tissue or periapical tooth.
Endocarditis prophylaxis is not recommended for procedures such as transesophageal echocardiography or gastrointestinal endoscopy, in the absence of active infection.
Clinical diagnosis of chronic AI can be made on the basis of the presence of an early diastolic murmur and a wide pulse pressure. C
The Austin Flint murmur (diastolic rumble auscultated in the precordium) is a highly specific (but difficult to detect) finding of chronic severe AI. C

Transthoracic echocardiogram confirms the diagnosis in most cases. A transesophageal echocardriogram is often indicated to identify the mechanism of severe aortic insufficiency, to confirm severity, and to plan for surgical therapy. C
Cardiac MRI, CT, or radionuclide ventriculography can be considered if echocardiogram results are inadequate. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Later onset of murmur. After P2, rather than A2. Normal pulse pressure.
Rare. Limited to 2nd/3rd intercostal space, lateral to left sternal border. Due to turbulent flow across moderately severe stenosis of the LAD artery.

list.listitem: See for diagnostic criteria.

American Society of Echocardiography criteria for the diagnosis of severe AI: (1) dense regurgitant jet, (2) effective regurgitant orifice area greater than or equal to 0.3 cm, (3) regurgitant volume greater than or equal to 60 mL/beat, (4) regurgitant fraction greater than or equal to 50%, (5) jet width greater than or equal to 65% of left ventricle outflow tract, and (6) vena contracta width greater than 0.6 cm. Other findings include diastolic flow reversal by Doppler in the descending thoracic aorta.

Chronic severe AI has a protracted asymptomatic phase during which the left ventricle gradually enlarges. Principal symptoms of exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea may not develop for years.

Diagnosis of chronic severe AI can usually be made on the basis of an early diastolic murmur along the left sternal border (3rd and 4th intercostal space) beginning immediately after A2. It is best heard with the patient sitting up and leaning forward.

Other findings may include a displaced left ventricle impulse (due to left ventricle enlargement), wide pulse pressure (due to aortic regurgitation), and characteristic signs of wide pulse pressure (eg, Corrigan's pulse, Quincke's sign, Duroziez's sign, and de Musset's sign). Most of these signs, however, have low diagnostic sensitivity and specificity.

An Austin Flint murmur is a highly specific finding in severe AI, although sensitivity is only modest. It is a low-pitched apical mid-diastolic murmur with a pre-systolic accentuation, heard best with the bell of the stethoscope with the patient in a left lateral position. The absence of an "opening snap" can differentiate it from the similar murmur of mitral stenosis.
In acute AI, the diastolic murmur may be short and/or soft, and the pulse pressure and left ventricle size may be normal.
Most of the characteristic clinical findings of chronic AI are modified or absent when valvular regurgitation is acute.
Electrocardiogram may show left ventricular (LV) hypertrophy, and cardiomegaly may be seen on chest x-ray. Dilatation of the ascending aorta and aortic arch is also often present.

Transthoracic echocardiography is considered the test of choice to assess the mechanism and severity of AI and should be performed in all patients suspected of having AI. Left ventricle size, systolic function, and aortic root size should also be assessed.
Cardiac MRI, CT, or radionuclide ventriculography can be considered to assess left ventricle size and function if transthoracic echocardiography is inadequate.

Cardiac catheterization with aortic root angiography is recommended if noninvasive testing does not adequately assess AI or left ventricle function, or if there is discrepancy between noninvasive findings and symptoms.

Recent studies correlate serum levels of B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) and pro-BNP with symptoms, severity of regurgitation, and degree of left ventricle dysfunction and may have prognostic value in patients who undergo cardiac surgery for AI.
A validated clinical rule can predict the need for pacing following valve surgery.
The diagnosis of AI can usually be made on the basis of a diastolic murmur and presence of a wide pulse pressure.

Echocardiogram is the key diagnostic test for confirming presence, quantifying severity, and assessing the mechanism of regurgitation. It also enables imaging of the aorta and the evaluation of left ventricle function.
See algorithm in .

Vasodilators like nifedipine, hydralazine, and angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors have been used in the treatment of symptomatic severe chronic AI in patients who are not surgical candidates. Results remain inconsistent and controversial. C
Aortic valve replacement is the definitive treatment for good surgical candidates with symptoms or left ventricle dysfunction/dilatation. B

Vasodilators should not be used in asymptomatic normotensive patients with mild-to-moderate chronic AI (see ). Their role remains controversial in long-term management of asymptomatic chronic severe AI. A recent meta-analysis of seven studies and 460 patients found benefit with vasodilator therapy in some measures of ventricular remodeling.

The calcium channel blocker nifedipine (30-120 mg per day) may decrease left ventricle volume and mass, and improve left ventricle function. Hydralazine and ACE inhibitors have also been used with mixed results.
The impact of vasodilators on long-term outcomes is uncertain, and improvement in hemodynamic and structural parameters is inconsistent.

Currently, β-blockers are generally contraindicated in chronic AI. However, a recent large observational study of 756 patients with severe AI showed that β-blocker therapy was an independent predictor of improved 1-year and 5-year survival rates.

The ACC/AHA guidelines recommends aortic valve replacement for the following indications: (1) symptomatic patients with severe chronic AI; and (2) asymptomatic patients with ( A ) left ventricle ejection fraction less than 50%, ( B ) left ventricle end-systolic dimension (LVESD) greater than 55 mm, or ( C ) left ventricle end-diastolic dimension (LVEDD) greater than 75 mm.

A randomized trial with 865 patients found that compared with interruption of therapy, continuation of anticoagulation for patients undergoing TAVI using long-term anticoagulant therapy may lead to more bleeding and vascular complications without the benefit of reducing thromboembolic events. Based on this study, holding anticoagulation prior to the procedure is recommended.

Surgery can also be considered in patients who have: (1) severe AI with evidence of progressive left ventricle dilatation; (2) an abnormal hemodynamic response to exercise and LVESD of 50 to 55 mm or LVEDD of 70 to 75 mm; and (3) who are undergoing cardiac surgery for other indications.
Emergent aortic valve replacement should be considered in most patients with acute AI.
A prospective cohort study found higher 15 year mortality among those receiving a biologic prosthesis compared with mechanical prosthesis (30.6% vs 26.%, HR 1.23, 95% CI 1.02-1.48).

Patients should be referred to a cardiologist if they are symptomatic, or if a transthoracic echocardiogram shows moderate to severe AI, left ventricle enlargement, left ventricle dysfunction, dilated aortic root, or a discrepancy between degree of AI and symptoms.
Hospitalization should be considered in patients with acute AI and when angina or symptoms of heart failure due to chronic AI cannot be adequately ameliorated in the outpatient setting.
Complications of AI include acute heart failure, chronic heart failure, and shock.
β-blockers (by prolonging diastolic time) and intra-aortic balloon pumps (by inflating during diastole) worsen regurgitation and are contraindicated in the management of shock because of acute AI.
Hospitalized patients with either acute or severe chronic AI may require IV vasodilators and diuretics to improve symptoms.
Chronic AI is characterized by a protracted asymptomatic phase. C
Once AI is diagnosed, patients should be followed up with serial clinical evaluations and echocardiography (). C

Poor prognosis is associated with development of symptoms, worse New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional class, increased left ventricle size and reduced left ventricle systolic function, and with acute AI in the absence of prompt surgical intervention. B
Even with severe AI, a long symptom-free interval is not unusual.
Sudden death can occur at a rate of 0.5% per year in these asymptomatic patients.
Asymptomatic patients with chronic AI and preserved left ventricle function progress to symptoms, left ventricle dysfunction, and death at an average rate of 4.3% per year (range = 2.1%-6.2%).
Development of symptoms is associated with poor prognosis. Poor prognosis is also associated with increased left ventricle size and reduced left ventricle systolic function.

Ten-year survival in asymptomatic individuals (NYHA class I) with AI is comparable with that of age-matched healthy patients, but 4-year survival is only 28% in patients with NYHA class III or IV heart failure.
Acute AI due to any cause, unless treated with prompt surgical intervention, will rapidly result in heart failure and death.
See for the recommended frequency of clinical and echocardiographic surveillance in patients with AI.

Repeat echocardiogram is indicated under the following circumstances: new onset of symptoms, increasing symptoms, decreasing exercise tolerance (exercise testing can also be considered), or clinical suggestion of worsening AI.
Follow-up after valve replacement.
For patients with a history of aortic valve replacement, patients should be advised on the use of prophylactic antibiotics before certain dental procedures.
Most patients with normal left ventricle function can participate in routine daily activities and mild-to-moderate exercise.
Increasing age is a risk factor for AI (OR = 2.3 for every 10-year increase in age).
AI in pregnancy is classified as either high risk or low risk.
High-risk features include NYHA class III or IV symptoms, left ventricle ejection fraction of less than 40%, and Marfan syndrome.
Low-risk features include NYHA class I or II symptoms or left ventricle ejection fraction of greater than 40%.
Pregnancy is usually uncomplicated and well tolerated in low-risk women.
Since cardiopulmonary bypass is associated with fetal complications, surgery should be avoided in pregnancy.
Termination of early pregnancies in high-risk women can be considered.
Alternatively, the patient can be managed medically until the fetus is viable, at which point cesarean should be the choice of delivery method.
Corrective surgery is recommended before subsequent attempts at pregnancy.

feature.caption: ACC/AHA Guideline on Vasodilator Therapy in Aortic Insufficiency.
feature.feature_body:
Class I – (evidence or general agreement for use)
Chronic treatment in patients with severe symptomatic AI who are not surgical candidates.
Class IIa – (weight of evidence is in favor or use)
Short-term treatment for hemodynamic improvement in patients with severe symptomatic AI before aortic valve (AV) replacement surgery.
Class IIb – (efficacy of use less well established)
Chronic treatment in patients with asymptomatic severe AI and left ventricular (LV) dilatation but with normal LV systolic function.
Class III – (therapy is not useful or may result in harm)
Chronic treatment in asymptomatic mild-moderate AI with normal LV systolic function. Chronic treatment in patients who are candidates for AV replacement surgery.
